title: Show a derivative satisfies a given relation

say: You give it a function $y$ and an equation that links $y$, $y'$ and $y''$. It **shows** the equation is true.
The key idea: find $y'$ and $y''$, put all three into the left side, and simplify until it equals the right side.

steps.title: Find the first derivative
steps.say: Use the product rule on $xe^{-2x}$ to find $\hl{1}{y'}$.

steps.title: Find the second derivative
steps.say: Differentiate $\hl{1}{y'}$ again to find $\hl{2}{y''}$. It is a product again.

steps.title: Simplify to zero
steps.say: Take out $e^{-2x}$ and collect the terms in the bracket.

lines.text: The left side equals $0$, the right side. So the equation is satisfied.

say: You give it quantities. It finds a **percentage**, a percentage change, or the original amount.
The key idea: turn the percentage into a **multiplier**. An increase of $8\%$ is $\times 1.08$. To undo it, divide.

example.question: The price of a bicycle was increased by $8\%$. It now costs €486. Find the original price.

steps.title: Write the new price as a percentage
steps.say: The original price is $100\%$. After the increase the price is $100\% + 8\%$ of the original.

steps.title: Divide by the multiplier
steps.say: €486 is $\hl{1}{1.08}$ times the original. To go back, divide by $\hl{1}{1.08}$.

steps.title: Check the answer
steps.say: Increase $\hl{2}{450}$ by $8\%$ and see if you get €486.

title: Change units (metric, imperial with factors, currency)

say: You give it a quantity and a conversion factor. It gives back the same quantity in **new units**.
The key idea: change one unit at a time. Multiply when the new unit is smaller, divide when it is bigger.

example.question: A train travels at $72$ km/h. Express its speed in metres per second.

steps.title: Change km to metres
steps.say: There are $1000$ metres in $1$ km. Multiply the distance by $\hl{1}{1000}$.

steps.title: Change hours to seconds
steps.say: There are $60 \times 60$ seconds in $1$ hour. So $72\,000$ m in $1$ hour is the same as $72\,000$ m in $\hl{2}{3600}$ s.

steps.title: Divide distance by time
steps.say: Metres per second is the distance in metres divided by the time in seconds.

title: Estimate, round and check order of magnitude

say: You give it a calculation. It gives back a quick **estimate**, close to the real answer, that you can do in your head.
The key idea: round every number to one **significant figure** first. Then the sum is easy, and the answer shows if your calculator work is sensible.

example.question:
A shop sells $19.8$ kg of cheese at $€6.10$ per kg.
(a) Estimate the cost by rounding each number to one significant figure.
(b) Calculate the exact cost.
(c) Is your answer to (b) sensible?

steps.title: Round each number
steps.say: Round each number to one significant figure. Keep the first digit that is not zero and round the rest.

steps.title: Multiply the rounded numbers
steps.say: Now multiply the easy numbers. This is the **estimate**.

steps.title: Calculate exactly
steps.say: Use the original numbers. Multiply the weight by the price per kg.

steps.title: Compare the two
steps.say: Put the exact answer next to the estimate. They should be close.

lines.text: The difference is under €1. The exact cost of $\hl{2}{€120.78}$ is sensible.

title: Calculate cost/selling price, discount, mark-up and margin

say: You give it a cost price and a selling price. It finds the **profit**, the **mark-up** and the **margin**.
The key idea: profit is selling price minus cost price. Mark-up is that profit as a percentage of the **cost price**. Margin is the same profit as a percentage of the **selling price**.

example.question: A shop buys a bag for $€45$ and sells it for $€60$. Find (a) the profit, (b) the mark-up as a percentage of the cost price, (c) the margin as a percentage of the selling price.

steps.title: Find the profit
steps.say: Profit is the selling price minus the cost price.

steps.title: Find the mark-up
steps.say: Mark-up divides the profit by the cost price. The cost price is the one the shop paid.

steps.title: Find the margin
steps.say: Margin divides the same profit by the selling price instead.

steps.title: Check the two
steps.say: The profit is the same in both. Only the number you divide by changes.

lines.text: Mark-up divides by $45$, the cost. Margin divides by $60$, the selling price.

say: You give it a starting amount $P$, a yearly rate and a number of years. It gives back the **final value** $F$.
The key idea: each year the amount is multiplied by the same number, $1 + i$. So after $t$ years you multiply $t$ times, which is $F = P(1 + i)^t$.

example.question: Aoife invests $€7000$ at $2.5\%$ per year compound interest for $3$ years. Find the value of her investment at the end of $3$ years, to the nearest cent.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Each year the amount grows by the rate. Write the formula for $t$ years.

steps.title: Write down what you know
steps.say: Change $2.5\%$ to a decimal. Then list the three values.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Put the numbers into the formula. Add $1$ to $\hl{1}{i}$ first.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.say: Work out the power, then multiply. Round to the cent at the end.

say: You give it a starting value $P$, a yearly rate of loss and a number of years. It gives back the **value** $F$ after those years.
The key idea: each year the value is multiplied by the same number, $1 - i$, because the car keeps $100\% - i$ of what it was worth. So $F = P(1 - i)^t$.

example.question: A van costs $€25\,000$ new. It loses $10\%$ of its value each year. Find the value of the van after $4$ years.

steps.title: Find the yearly multiplier
steps.say: The van keeps $90\%$ of its value each year. Write that as a decimal.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Each year the value is multiplied by $\hl{2}{0.9}$. After $t$ years that is $t$ times.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Put in $P = 25\,000$, the multiplier $\hl{2}{0.9}$ and $t = 4$.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.say: Work out $0.9^4$, then multiply.

title: Convert between annual and periodic rates (AER/APR)

say: You give it a rate for one period, such as a yearly rate. It gives back the **equivalent** rate for a different period, such as a month.
The key idea: growth multiplies. Twelve months of growth at rate $i$ must give the same result as one year at the annual rate, so $(1+i)^{12} = 1 + \text{annual rate}$.

example.question: A bank quotes an annual percentage rate (APR) of $3.6\%$. Find the equivalent monthly rate, correct to 3 significant figures.

steps.title: Set up the equation
steps.say: One year is $12$ months. Growth at the monthly rate $\hl{1}{i}$ twelve times must equal the growth at the annual rate.

steps.title: Take the 12th root
steps.say: To undo the power of $12$, raise both sides to the power $\frac{1}{12}$.

steps.title: Subtract 1
steps.say: Take away the $1$ to leave $\hl{1}{i}$ alone, then write it as a percentage.

title: Calculate income tax, USC, PRSI and net pay

say: You give it a gross pay, the tax rates and bands, and the tax credits. It gives back the **gross tax**, the **net tax** and the **net pay**.
The key idea: each rate applies only to its own slice of the pay, and the tax credits come off the tax, not off the pay.

example.question: Ciara earns $€56\,000$ a year. She pays tax at $20\%$ on the first $€42\,000$ and $40\%$ on the rest. Her tax credits are $€3\,500$. Find her net pay.

steps.title: Tax at the 20% rate
steps.say: The $20\%$ rate applies only to the first $€42\,000$.

steps.title: Tax at the 40% rate
steps.say: The rest of the pay is what is left after the first $€42\,000$. Tax that at $40\%$.

steps.title: Add to get gross tax
steps.say: Add the two amounts to get the $\hl{1}{\text{gross tax}}$.

steps.title: Take off the credits
steps.say: The credits come off the tax. What is left is the $\hl{2}{\text{net tax}}$.

steps.title: Find the net pay
steps.say: Take the $\hl{2}{\text{net tax}}$ from the gross pay.

lines.text: Only the tax is reduced by the credits. The pay is not.

say: You give it a job: the amounts of materials, the price of each, the wastage and the labour. It gives back the **total cost**.
The key idea: cost each part of the job on its own, then add them. Wastage means buying more than you need, so the amount goes up by that percentage.

example.question: A room is $5$ m by $4$ m. The floor is to be tiled. Tiles cost $€30$ per m², and $8\%$ extra is bought for wastage. The tiler charges $€45$ per hour for $6$ hours. Find the total cost.

steps.title: Area of the floor
steps.say: Multiply the length by the width.

steps.title: Add the wastage
steps.say: $8\%$ extra means $108\%$ of the area. Multiply by $1.08$.

steps.title: Cost of the tiles
steps.say: Multiply the area to buy by the price per m². This is the cost of the $\hl{1}{\text{tiles}}$.

steps.title: Cost of the labour
steps.say: Multiply the hours by the rate per hour to get the $\hl{2}{\text{labour}}$.

steps.title: Add for the total
steps.say: Add the $\hl{1}{\text{tiles}}$ and the $\hl{2}{\text{labour}}$.

title: Calculate percentage error, tolerance and accumulated error

say: You give it an estimated value and the true value. It gives back the **percentage error**: how far off the estimate is, as a percentage of the truth.
The key idea: the error is the difference between the two values, and you always divide it by the **true** value.

example.question: A table is measured as $1.46$ m long. The true length is $1.50$ m. Find the percentage error, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the error
steps.say: The error is the difference between the true value and the estimate.

steps.title: Divide by the true value
steps.say: Divide the $\hl{1}{\text{error}}$ by the true value, $1.50$. Multiply by $100$ to make it a percentage.

steps.title: Round the answer
steps.say: Round to one decimal place and write the percent sign.

title: Calculate an average rate of change over time

say: You give it a change in some quantity and the time it took. It finds the **rate**: how much the quantity changes in each unit of time.
The key idea: rate is change divided by time. For a journey in parts, add up the total change and the total time first, then divide once.

example.question: A cyclist rides $18$ km in $45$ minutes, then $12$ km in $15$ minutes. Find her average speed for the whole journey, in km/h.

steps.title: Change minutes to hours
steps.say: Speed in km/h needs the time in **hours**. Divide each number of minutes by $60$.

steps.title: Add the totals
steps.say: Do not average the two speeds. Add up the whole distance and the whole time.

steps.title: Divide distance by time
steps.say: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.

lines.text: The two speeds were $24$ and $48$ km/h. The average is not $36$, because she spent longer at the slower speed.
